extracted.intended_audience: students and contestants preparing for mathematical olympiads / recreational problem solvers (high-school to early-college level)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter of problems and solutions illustrating the Invariance Principle: identify quantities (parity, residues, weights, gcd, products, color counts, etc.) that remain unchanged or monotone under allowed moves to prove reachability or impossibility. Contains many combinatorial/number-theoretic/geometry puzzle examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity of number of odd persons (handshakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The parity (evenness) of the count of people who have exchanged an odd number of handshakes is preserved throughout the handshake process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two odd persons shake, the number of odd persons increases by 2; if two even persons shake, it decreases by 2; if one odd and one even shake, it stays the same. Since initially there are 0 odd persons, the number of odd persons is always even (Problem 32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity of odd integers under pair replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: When replacing pairs of integers by other pairs in certain moves, the parity (even/odd) of the count of odd integers is invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replacing two odd integers decreases odd count by 2; replacing one odd and one even or two evens leaves odd count unchanged. Used to show one even remains (Solution to Problem 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminant invariance for quadratic polynomial transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the specific transformations f(x) → x^2 f(1/x + 1) and f(x) → (x − 1)^2 f[1/(x − 1)], the discriminant b^2 − 4ac of a quadratic ax^2 + bx + c remains invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the discriminant after each transformation to see it equals the original discriminant; therefore polynomials with different discriminants cannot be transformed into one another (Problem 34: x^2+4x+3 has discriminant 4, x^2+10x+9 has 64 ⇒ impossible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity of inversion count under neighbor swaps
rubrics_metrics.description: The parity (even/odd) of the number of inversions in a permutation changes predictably under swaps of adjacent elements; adjacent swaps change inversion parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define U as sum, for each 1, of number of 0s to its right (or inversions generally). An adjacent interchange changes parity of U. Used to show certain states cannot be reached (Problems 33, 36, 37, 38).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight assignment invariant for chip splitting on lattice
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning weight 1/2^{x+y} to square with lower-left corner (x,y) yields a total weight that is invariant under operation: remove chip at (x,y) and place chips at (x+1,y) and (x,y+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute total board weight and compare weight of shaded region vs. available weight to show impossibility of clearing shaded squares in finite moves (Problem 39).

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm/weight monotone for solitaire jumps (golden-ratio weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define norm n(x,y)=|x|+|y−5| and weight α^{n} where α is the positive root of α^2+α−1=0; total weight is nonincreasing under allowed jumps (some jumps preserve weight, others decrease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total weight of any finite initial configuration on/below the x-axis is <1 while target (0,5) has weight 1, so target unreachable (Problem 40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity pattern of coordinates under point reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection of a point X at a lattice point A maps coordinates (x,y,z) → (2a−x,2b−y,2c−z), preserving parity of each coordinate; hence the parity pattern of coordinate vectors is invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting with seven cube vertices with certain parity patterns, you can never produce the vertex with all coordinates odd (1,1,1) (Problem 41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Color-parity invariant for jumps on colored board (three-coloring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Color the board cyclically with three colors A,B,C; the parities (mod 2) of counts of occupied squares of each color change together so their congruence class (a ≡ b ≡ c mod 2) is invariant under jumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show an n×n board divisible by 3 cannot be reduced to one chip (Problem 42): a ≡ b ≡ c mod 2 initially, and a single remaining chip would violate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perimeter nonincreasing under infection spread
rubrics_metrics.description: When cells with at least two infected neighbors become infected, the perimeter of the infected region does not increase (may decrease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial perimeter bound prevents infection from reaching states requiring larger perimeter (Problem 43: initial ≤36 cannot reach 40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum modulo n invariant for circular chip transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: For chips on a circle, S = ∑ i a_i (weighted by positions) is invariant modulo n under allowed moves (each move changes S by 0 or ±n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end, S must be congruent to 0 mod n; use this to decide reachability based on initial S (Problem 22).

rubrics_metrics.name: gcd invariance (or controlled change) under specific moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain move rules leave gcd(x,y) unchanged or multiply it by 2; the gcd (or its parity/divisibility properties) is an invariant controlling reachability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., permitted moves either leave gcd(x,y) invariant or double it; reachability characterized by gcd conditions (Problems 15, 20, 27).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear combination invariant modulo base (example mod 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific linear combination of variables (e.g., I = 2x1 + 4x2 + 6x3 + 8x4 + 10x5 + 12x6) is invariant modulo a base under the move rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute I mod 10 initially and for the goal state to show impossibility when residues differ (Problem 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone invariant (sum of squares decreases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some processes admit a monotone measure (e.g., sum of squares of components) that strictly decreases with each nontrivial move until a stable configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using inequalities one shows the sum of squares strictly decreases unless all entries equal; hence the process terminates and certain final states are impossible (Problem 23, Solution 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of reciprocals nonincreasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain averaging and replacement operations, S = ∑ 1/x_i does not increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inequality 1/a + 1/b ≥ 4/(a+b) to show S is nonincreasing and bound the final possible value (Problem 28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of polygon side directions and finiteness via area increase
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflections that keep side directions invariant cause area to strictly increase with each step while the set of possible side sequences is finite, implying process terminates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show reflecting a polygon repeatedly yields a finite process (Problem 29); note for line reflections the directions may change and the argument is harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-point inheritance under composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x) = x (x a fixed point of f), then f(f(x)) = x; fixed points of f are fixed points of f∘f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solving f(f(x)) = x, first find fixed points of f, factor the polynomial accordingly, and then search for additional periodic points (Problem 30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product invariant for ± signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing two signs by + if equal and − if unequal corresponds to multiplying mapped values (+→1, −→−1); the product of all numbers is invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute product P of ±1 representations; P is unchanged by the replacement rule, so final sign cannot depend on elimination order (Problem 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital sum modulo 9 invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital sum (sum of digits) modulo 9 is invariant under certain digit permutations/operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use congruence mod 9 to rule out configurations that would force a conflicting digital sum (Problems 9 and 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between white and black sums invariant under neighbor-add operations
rubrics_metrics.description: When allowed operation is adding the same integer to two neighboring numbers, the difference between total sums on white and black squares (W − B) remains invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare W − B for initial and target configurations to decide reachability (Problem 48: 5 cannot become −1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant linear/algebraic relations from move definitions (closure tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: When moves are described by deterministic replacement rules (e.g., letter-reduction table or binary operation ◦), the algebraic structure yields invariants ensuring the final outcome does not depend on order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replacement rules among e,a,b form an operation with properties that show the last letter is order-independent (Problem 50); similar reasoning applies to other reduction systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working backwards as a problem-solving principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve reachability problems by reasoning backward from goal states to possible predecessors, using invariants to limit choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly (explicitly noted in Problem 5 and elsewhere); e.g., if final state must come from a uniquely determined previous state, backtracking shows impossibility or constructs a sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modular invariants (remainders) to rule out possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Remainders modulo an integer (e.g., mod 2, mod 3, mod n) of some aggregated quantity are invariant under allowed moves and can preclude certain target states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many examples: sums modulo 2 or 3 excluding certain rows/columns (Problem 13), using remainders mod 9 (Problems 9, 14), or other moduli in reachability arguments.
